newsitem.title: BRAZIL: Britain closes in on Biggs with new Brazil treaty.
newsitem.headline: Britain closes in on Biggs with new Brazil treaty.

text.p: Britain took a step toward recapturing its best-known criminal fugitive, Ronnie Biggs, when it ratified a long-awaited extradition treaty with Brazil on Wednesday.

Diplomatic officials met at Brazil's Foreign Ministry to exchange documents in a simple ceremony that could mean the end of more than 30 years on the run for Biggs, a member of the gang that carried out the legendary "Great Train Robbery" in 1963.

British Ambassador Keith Haskell said that while the treaty paved the way for an extradition request for Biggs, none had been made by London. "It's now up to the Home Office (Interior Ministry)," he told reporters.

Haskell also said he did not expect Biggs to be whisked back to Britain soon, because any extradition request would have to be approved by Brazil's high court. "This process can take quite a long time," the ambassador said.
Britain and Brazil first signed the extradition treaty in 1995, but its terms had to approved by the parliaments of each country, a process that took two years.
Biggs, who has become a minor celebrity since arriving in Brazil as an escaped convict in 1970, was keeping an unusually low profile.

"At the present moment, I'm not prepared to make any statement on my future," the 68-year-old Biggs said by telephone from his home in Rio de Janeiro shortly before the treaty was ratified. "I'm acting on my lawyers' advice on this."

In a recent interview with Reuters, however, he said he was confident he would continue to give British justice the slip. "I have infinite faith I won't go to jail," he said. "I have been lucky until today, and I hope I will continue to be lucky."

Biggs was sentenced to a 30-year term for his part in robbing 2.6 million pounds -- the equivalent of $50 million today -- from a Glasgow-to-London postal train. He escaped from a prison in London after serving only 15 months and underwent plastic surgery in Australia before ending up in Rio.
Describing himself as broke, Biggs says he lives off royalties from a recent autobiography and fees paid by tourists to attend barbecues at his home.

Biggs and his lawyers were expected to use an array of legal arguments to counter any move by Britain to put him back in prison, including the fact that in Brazil crimes committed more than 20 years ago are considered not to have taken place.
